title: Traversing Indices and Justifying Every Access

blocks.text: A range-based loop provides each value. If we need to display its position, compare neighbors, or visit only part of the collection, we can use a for loop with an index. The access rule stays the same: before reading datos[i], we must know that i is less than size() and represents a nonnegative position.

For the sizes and indices of our vectors we will use std::size_t, available through <cstddef>. It is an unsigned integer type: it represents zero and positive quantities within a finite range. It cannot represent a negative index. Using it here keeps the types consistent with these collections' sizes; that does not make it suitable for every quantity in a program.
The output is 0:8;1:3;2:6;. The condition is checked before every access. When i reaches three, it is false and the body no longer runs.

blocks.question: Predict the exact output, without adding quotation marks.
blocks.explanation: There are two valid indices, zero and one.

blocks.question: Fill in only the comparison operator that requires i to be strictly less than datos.size().
blocks.explanation: < prevents the body from running when i equals size().

blocks.question: Why does i <= datos.size() fail to protect this access?
options: Because it allows i to equal the size, which is not a valid position.
Because it always starts at one.
blocks.explanation: The upper bound of the valid range is excluded. We do not run the version using <=.

blocks.question: Predict the exact output, without adding quotation marks.
blocks.explanation: Zero is not less than zero. No access takes place.

blocks.question: Predict the exact output, without adding quotation marks.
blocks.explanation: The only existing position is zero.

blocks.text: We do not habitually store size() in int: a general collection could have a size that does not fit in that type. Our examples keep indices and sizes in an appropriate type and small sums of element values in int when suitable.
Compare neighboring elements without inventing a predecessor

To compare datos[i] with datos[i - 1], we start at i = 1. The previous position zero then exists. The condition i < size() ensures that the current position exists. In an empty collection or a one-element collection there are no neighboring pairs, so the body runs zero times.

blocks.question: Predict the exact output, without adding quotation marks.
blocks.explanation: The pairs at positions 0/1 and 2/3 match. We are not counting globally distinct values.

blocks.question: With one element, how many neighboring pairs are compared?
blocks.explanation: A pair requires two positions; starting at one avoids inventing a previous neighbor.

blocks.question: Fill in only the starting digit and the name of the size operation used to compare neighbors.

blocks.text: Traverse backward with a count of remaining elements

The previous solution starts at one and uses size(). To move backward, we will not use i >= 0 as a condition with an unsigned integer: that condition never detects a negative value, and subtracting from zero does not yield the -1 you might expect. We can count the elements remaining: cuenta starts at size(), and only when cuenta > 0 do we access cuenta - 1.

blocks.question: Predict the exact output, without adding quotation marks.
blocks.explanation: The counts are three, two, and one; their indices are two, one, and zero.

blocks.question: What makes subtracting cuenta - 1 safe inside this body?
options: An unsigned integer can always represent -1.
Subtracting creates a new vector element.
The condition cuenta > 0 has already been satisfied.
blocks.explanation: With a positive count, the subtraction identifies an existing index and the count does not exceed the size.

blocks.question: Predict the exact output, without adding quotation marks.
blocks.explanation: The condition refers to the index: positions zero and two change, not every even-valued element.

blocks.question: You must increase even values, regardless of their positions. What should the condition inspect?
blocks.explanation: Index and value have different meanings even though both are numbers.

blocks.text: We do not grow the vector during these traversals. Every example uses a finite collection prepared before the loop, and all accesses remain within its valid range.

Build a report using {3, 7, 1}: display Session 1: 3, Session 2: 7, and Session 3: 1 on separate lines. The index starts at zero, but the label shown to a person starts at one. Then test {} and {0}: the empty vector displays no sessions; the single zero displays Session 1: 0. Do not access an additional index just to print the last line.
As a second variation, display only the values in reverse order, separated by semicolons. Explain in writing the first and last positions of both traversals.
Reference solution and review of loop conditions

blocks.question: Predict the exact output, without adding quotation marks.
blocks.explanation: A count of one allows index zero; then the loop ends without subtracting from zero inside the body.

blocks.question: What must you preserve when changing a loop condition?
options: That there are always three visits.
The justification that all used indices exist and that the loop terminates.
blocks.explanation: The condition determines which visits are possible and when the traversal ends.

blocks.text: Lab criteria: every used index must be within bounds; the human-readable label and index must preserve the specified relationship; an empty vector must produce zero visits; the reverse variation must stop before subtracting from a count of zero.
